title: SYSK Selects: How Dying Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode "How Dying Works." Josh and Chuck walk through the physiology and social side of death: how humans have defined death over time (from the soul departing the body, to the Harvard brain death definition, to the whole-brain definition in the Uniform Determination of Death Act), the common ways people die (heart attack, drowning, bleeding out, electrocution, falls, fire, hanging, old age/frailty), the pre-active and active dying phases (Cheyne-Stokes breathing, death rattle, hearing lasting longest, lacrimal mortis, tache noire), what happens after death (algor, livor and rigor mortis, decomposition, purge fluid, coffin birth, degloving), palliative and hospice care, assisted suicide debates (including Sigmund Freud and Hunter Thompson), and a list of common life regrets. The episode ends with a listener mail about spider flashlight tricks and a shout-out.

segments.title: Rerun intro and population banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Selects rerun of How Dying Works and explains its listener feedback. He and Chuck banter, and Josh cites a Population Reference Bureau estimate that about 107 billion humans have ever lived, noting death as the one common thread.

segments.title: Ernest Becker and the show's prior death coverage
segments.summary: The hosts reference Ernest Becker's The Denial of Death and list past death-related episodes. They introduce the idea that the episode will focus on how dying works physiologically.

segments.title: Historical definitions of death
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how death was once defined as the soul leaving the body, and how signs like feathers and mirrors, and later the stethoscope and the Ballistocardiograph-style needle test, were used to check for death. Modern medical technology has complicated the definition.

segments.title: Brain death and whole brain definition
segments.summary: Coma depasse, persistent vegetative state and irreversible coma are introduced. Harvard's higher-brain criteria are contrasted with the whole-brain definition adopted in the Uniform Determination of Death Act after a presidential commission.

segments.title: Organ transplants and the death definition
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how transplant advances in the 1960s pressured the definition of death, and how most developed countries adopted whole-brain criteria.

segments.title: Ways people die: accident, violence, natural causes
segments.summary: The hosts outline three categories of death: accidental, violent (homicide or suicide), and natural. They describe what drowning, heart attack, blood loss, electrocution, falls, hanging and burning are like, and note that heart disease and cancer are leading US causes of death.

segments.title: Old age, frailty, and the dying timeline
segments.summary: Old age death is described as a modern prominent form of death, called frailty. The body shuts down gradually and the hosts introduce the pre-active phase (weeks before death) and the active dying phase (days).

segments.title: Symptoms in the pre-active and active dying phases
segments.summary: Signs described include sleepiness, cooling skin, mottling, withdrawal, patients saying they are dying, loss of bladder control, Cheyne-Stokes breathing, hallucinated visitors, death rattle, convulsions, and the sequence in which senses fade, with hearing lasting longest.

segments.title: Family support, eyes, and immediate death signs
segments.summary: Hosts advise families on being around dying people, including comforting words and calm environments. They then cover pupils dilating, lacrimal mortis (final tear), and tache noire, and why eyes should be closed.

segments.title: Postmortem changes: cooling, rigor, decomposition
segments.summary: The hosts describe the body after death: microbiome and skin cells, algor mortis, livor mortis, rigor mortis, and decomposition with bloating, purge fluid, and coffin birth (postmortem fetal extrusion). They also mention degloving from airbags.

segments.title: Palliative care, hospice, and assisted suicide
segments.summary: Hosts discuss palliative and hospice care, the tendency for people to die in ICUs, advance directives, and the debate over physician-assisted suicide, including Sigmund Freud's and Hunter Thompson's deaths.

segments.title: Common life regrets
segments.summary: A hospice nurse's list of five common regrets is read, including living true to oneself, working too hard, expressing feelings, staying in touch with friends, and letting oneself be happier.

segments.title: Closing and wrap-up of death series
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the death series and point to the website and search for more death content.

segments.title: Listener mail: spider flashlight trick and shout-out
segments.summary: A listener thanks the hosts for the flashlight trick for seeing spiders at night and asks for a shout-out to her fiance before their wedding.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close with social media and contact info.
